To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

infectious and parasitic diseases are a leading cause of human cancer, that primary prevention is addressed to the avoidance and eradication, and that vaccines are fundamental tools to prevent infection-related cancers.

(a) chronic infections with H.pylori, HPV, HBV/HCV, and EBV are associated with human cancers; (b) the large-scale application of vaccines has already shown to reduce the incidence of infection-related cancers; (c) the detection of early gastric cancer has been applied in some Asian countries; (d) the secondary prevention has been applied in the control of HPV-related cancers; (e) the tertiary prevention has been applied to avoid local relapses, invas
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of new infectious agents, their role in the etiology of cancer, the development of new diagnostic tools, and the application of prevention and treatment strategies.
the development and evaluation of novel prevention strategies, such as vaccination and chemoprevention, for the control of cancer of infectious origin.
the identification of the etiological agents of human cancer and the development of effective prevention strategies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, although the prevention of infection-related cancer has already found broad application, the potential of primary and secondary prevention is still largely unexploited.
, in addition to the well-established role of tobacco and alcohol in the development of cancer, the infectious agents and parasites are responsible for the 15% to 20% of all human malignancies.
, while primary prevention of infection-associated cancer is feasible and should be implemented, secondary and tertiary prevention strategies are not yet available for most of these cancers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have to continue our efforts to identify the etiological agents for cancer, develop vaccines to prevent the diseases caused by them and to treat the diseases by using specific agents.
, although the role of infectious agents in the pathogenesis of cancer has been recognized for many decades, the molecular mechanisms of infection-related carcinogenesis are still poorly understood.
, while primary and secondary prevention are the most effective means of cancer control, tertiary prevention can be used to improve the efficacy of the other two.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a large proportion of human cancers is associated with chronic infections.
the prevention of cancer is feasible and that a large number of cancers of infectious origins can be prevented or cured by the application of vaccines and/or other preventive strategies.
the prevention of infection-related human cancers is a realistic goal.
